features.doc: The routes to weak necessity are a dedicated item, a strong modal with weakening morphology, and evaluative comparative language.

levels.name: lexical
levels.label: lexical
levels.doc: A dedicated weak necessity modal, English *ought*

levels.name: compositional
levels.label: compositional
levels.doc: A strong necessity modal with counterfactual morphology, Spanish *debería*

examples.primaryText: I don't think you should leave.
examples.context: Embedded under 'I don't think', testing the lower-negation (neg-raising) reading.
examples.comment: Horn (1978, p. 198) ex. (31a): 'I don't think you should leave' is paraphrasable as 'I think you should stay' — the lower-negation (THINK > NOT > should) reading is available for weak necessity should.

examples.primaryText: I don't think you ought to leave.
examples.context: Embedded under 'I don't think', testing the lower-negation (neg-raising) reading.
examples.comment: Horn (1978, p. 198) ex. (31a): weak necessity 'ought to' admits the lower-negation reading 'I think you ought to stay'.

examples.primaryText: I don't think you better leave.
examples.context: Embedded under 'I don't think', testing the lower-negation (neg-raising) reading.
examples.comment: Horn (1978, p. 198) ex. (31a): the comparative evaluative 'better' ('(had) better' in the prose) neg-raises, paraphrasable as 'I think you better stay'.

examples.primaryText: It wouldn't be good for you to cheat on your taxes.
examples.context: Negated evaluative; tests the excluded-middle (neg-raising) inference under higher negation.
examples.comment: Horn (1978, p. 211) ex. (30): 'It wouldn't be good for you to cheat' is read as 'It would be good for you not to cheat' — modal 'good' neg-raises.

examples.primaryText: I don't think you must leave.
examples.context: Embedded under 'I don't think', testing whether the lower-negation reading is available for a strong necessity modal.
examples.comment: Horn (1978, p. 198) ex. (31b): strong necessity 'must' does NOT support the lower-negation reading — 'I don't think you must leave' is not equivalent to 'I think you must stay'.

examples.primaryText: I don't think you have to leave.
examples.context: Embedded under 'I don't think', testing whether the lower-negation reading is available for a strong necessity modal.
examples.comment: Horn (1978, p. 198) ex. (31b): strong necessity 'have to' lacks the lower-negation reading; negation can only be interpreted in the matrix clause.

examples.primaryText: ce'irim sinim kayom lo xošvim še-'adif axeret.
examples.translation: (I'm astonished that) young Chinese these days don't think it would be better if things were different.
examples.context: Blog discussion of attitudes; tests neg-raising (cyclicity) of 'adif 'preferable' in Hebrew.
examples.comment: Rubinstein (2014) ex. (33): 'adif 'preferable' shows the neg-raising (cyclicity) reading in Hebrew — negation interpreted narrowly under the evaluative comparative (THINK > PREFERABLE > NOT).

examples.primaryText: I ought to do the dishes but I don't have to.
examples.context: Test 1 (x E q, but doesn't have to q) with lexical weak-necessity 'ought'.
examples.comment: Rubinstein (2014) ex. (8a), 'Lexical WN': English dedicates a lexical item (ought/should) to weak necessity. Passes Test 1 — felicitous because weak necessity is strictly weaker than have-to.

examples.primaryText: Debería limpiar los platos, pero no estoy obligado.
examples.translation: I ought to do the dishes but I am not obliged to.
examples.context: Spanish derives weak necessity compositionally: strong modal deber + conditional morphology.
examples.comment: Rubinstein (2014) ex. (8b), 'Compositional WN' (von Fintel & Iatridou 2008, p. 122): Spanish builds weak necessity from a strong necessity modal (deber) plus the conditional morphology characteristic of counterfactual consequents. The paper prints Deberia (/Tendria que), without the accent.

examples.primaryText: hu carix lištof et ha-kelim, aval hu lo xayav.
examples.translation: He needs to do the dishes, but he doesn't have to.
examples.context: Given the rules of the house. Test 1 (x ought to q, but doesn't have to) with carix 'need' substituted for ought.
examples.comment: Rubinstein (2014) ex. (16a): substituting carix 'need' for ought yields a contradiction in Test 1 — carix aligns with strong necessity (xayav 'must'), so 'needs to but doesn't have to' is infelicitous.

examples.primaryText: melcarim xayavim lištof yadayim, aval orxim raq crxim.
examples.translation: Waiters have to wash their hands, but guests only need to.
examples.context: Test 2 with the exclusive 'only' (raq): y has to q, x only need-to q.
examples.comment: Rubinstein (2014) ex. (19): 'Test 2 with an exclusive' — carix 'need' does not set up a felicitous scalar contrast against xayav 'must', confirming it is not a weak necessity modal.

examples.primaryText: yoter tov še-hu yitpater, aval hu lo xayav lehitpater.
examples.translation: It is better that he resign, but he doesn't have to resign.
examples.context: Bribe scenario: a convicted politician ought to resign though no law requires it. Hebrew renders weak-necessity 'ought' via morphological comparison (yoter tov 'more good').
examples.comment: Rubinstein (2014) ex. (21a): Hebrew, lacking a lexical weak-necessity modal, translates priority-type 'ought' with the morphological comparative yoter/haxi tov 'more/most good'. Passes Test 1.

examples.primaryText: 'adif še-hu yitpater, aval hu lo xayav lehitpater.
examples.translation: It is preferable that he resign, but he doesn't have to resign.
examples.context: Bribe scenario; lexical comparison with a predicate of preference, 'adif 'preferable'.
examples.comment: Rubinstein (2014) ex. (21b): lexical comparison with the predicate of preference 'adif 'preferable'.

examples.primaryText: kday še-hu yitpater, aval hu lo xayav lehitpater.
examples.translation: It would be good that he resign, but he doesn't have to resign.
examples.context: Bribe scenario; implicit comparison with evaluative predicates kday 'worthwhile' / ra'uy 'fitting'.
examples.comment: Rubinstein (2014) ex. (21c): implicit comparison with evaluative predicates kday 'worthwhile' / ra'uy 'fitting'.

examples.primaryText: It would be better that the politician gets himself fired than that he keep working, but he really ought to quit voluntarily.
examples.context: Three salient alternatives (get fired / keep working / resign). The morphological comparative pairwise-compares two of them.
examples.comment: Rubinstein (2014) ex. (24) (Julia Staffel, p.c.): the morphological comparative 'better' supports an explicit than-clause comparing two alternatives, whereas modal 'ought' (positive/superlative) only selects the overall best. The comparative backbone is overt in the than-clause.

examples.primaryText: ani lo xoševet še-ata carix lihyot po
examples.translation: I don't think you should be here.
examples.context: The speaker tries to prevent someone from entering a meeting they are not invited to.
examples.comment: Read as 'I think you shouldn't be here': the paper's apparent exception to the rule that strong necessity modals do not neg-raise, tied to the hybrid nature of carix.
